title: L2 versus L3, routing tables and longest prefix match
summary: The forwarding decision in detail: what changes at each hop, how a Linux routing table is structured, and how longest prefix match actually resolves.

sections.heading: What changes at each hop
sections.html:
FieldSwitch (L2)Router (L3)
Source MACUnchangedRewritten to the egress interface
Destination MACUsed for lookup; unchangedRewritten to the next hop's MAC
Source/destination IPNot readRead for the lookup; dest unchanged (except NAT)
TTLNot present in a frameDecremented; dropped at 0
BroadcastFlooded within VLANNot forwarded

So a packet's IP header is essentially stable end to end, while its frame header is rewritten at every hop. Anything that mangles that (asymmetric routing, NAT, tunnels) changes what you can infer from a capture.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Linux routing table
sections.html:
$ ip routedefault via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp src 192.168.1.42 metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.42 metric 100
10.8.0.0/24 via 10.8.0.1 dev tun0 metric 50
203.0.113.0/24 dev eth1 proto static scope link metric 20
ColumnMeaning
default0.0.0.0/0 — the catch-all
viaNext-hop IP; absent means the destination is on-link
devEgress interface
proto kernelInstalled automatically from the interface's address/mask
proto dhcpInstalled from a DHCP option
proto staticConfigured by an administrator
scope linkDestination is on this link; no gateway needed
scope hostLocal address (127.0.0.1/8, own addresses)
metricPreference between routes to the same prefix from the same source

Note the order of authority in Linux: longest prefix first; then route type (a more specific or hand-configured route beats a learned one); then metric. Multiple default routes with different metrics give you a crude failover: the lower metric wins, and if its interface goes down the route is withdrawn.

sections.heading: Longest prefix match, worked
sections.html:
Table:

0.0.0.0/0     via 192.168.1.1     metric 100
10.0.0.0/8    via 10.8.0.1        metric 50
10.1.0.0/16   via 10.8.0.2        metric 50
10.1.2.0/24   dev eth1            metric 20
DestinationMatching prefixesWinnerWhy
10.1.2.55/0, /8, /16, /24/24 on eth1Most specific; sent directly, no gateway
10.1.5.9/0, /8, /16/16 via 10.8.0.2/16 beats /8 despite the same metric
10.9.0.1/0, /8/8 via 10.8.0.1/8 beats default
8.8.8.8/0defaultNothing else matches

The trap to remember for interviews: metric never overrides specificity. A /24 with a terrible metric still beats a /8 with a perfect one.

Verify any claim with:

ip route get 10.1.5.9

sections.heading: Routing loops and convergence
sections.html:
A loop exists when two routers each believe the other is the better path to a destination. Symptoms: TTL exhaustion (visible as ICMP time-exceeded from each other), traceroute showing the same addresses repeating, and latency that increases in steps.

Loops come from stale information — a link failed but a router still advertises the old path. Link-state protocols flood new information quickly and reconverge; distance-vector protocols need mechanisms to stop counting to infinity (split horizon, poison reverse, triggered updates). Convergence is simply 'everyone has the same, current view'. Every routing incident you will ever debug is a convergence failure or a policy misconfiguration.

checks.prompt: What does `ip route get 203.0.113.9` print, and why is it useful?
options: The ARP entry for the destination
The route, source address and interface the kernel would use — without sending traffic
checks.explanation: It performs the same lookup the kernel would perform for a real packet and prints the decision, including the chosen source IP.

why_wrong.2: It shows the decision, not reachability.

checks.prompt: A host has default via 192.168.1.1 (metric 100) and 172.16.0.0/12 dev eth1 (metric 500). A packet to 172.16.5.5 goes where?
options: Out eth1 directly, because /12 is more specific than /0
To the default gateway, because metric 100 is better
checks.explanation: Specificity is evaluated first. The connected /12 matches, so the packet goes out eth1 regardless of its worse metric.

why_wrong.2: Metric only compares routes to the same prefix.
why_wrong.1: One route is selected per packet.
why_wrong.3: There is no conflict; the order of evaluation is defined.

connect.title: Switching
connect.text: Each routed hop re-resolves the next hop's MAC — switching and routing alternate on the same wire.

connect.title: IP addressing
connect.text: Connected and local routes are generated from the interface address and mask; change the mask and the table changes.

connect.title: Case study 8
connect.text: The routing misconfiguration mission is a longest-prefix-match puzzle with a real symptom.

interview.a: The router collects every table entry whose prefix contains the destination and selects the one with the longest mask. Specificity is evaluated before metric or administrative distance, so a more-specific route always wins.

interview.q: What is the difference between a static and a dynamic route?
interview.a: A static route is configured by an administrator and never changes unless a human or a script changes it. A dynamic route is learned by a routing protocol that reacts to topology changes, which is what allows convergence and failover at scale.
